issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: For a refugee trauma profile, comments on sexual violence are too trauma-specific and suggest a sexual assault formulation that is not otherwise supported by the threat, memory, or appraisal items. Nothing else in the profile indicates sexual trauma content, making this trigger hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: Avoiding situations where others evaluate appearance/performance fits social-evaluative shame concerns, but the rest of the profile centers on danger, distrust, intrusive sensory recall, and hypervigilance rather than evaluation-based threat. This strategy is not well linked to the active trigger/threat/appraisal pattern and is clinically out of place.

vignette:
Sofia, a 34-year-old Latin American woman, became a prison guard in the American Southwest five years after fleeing her home country. The traumatic event that set her on this path occurred at a military checkpoint during a period of civil unrest. Soldiers in dusty fatigues yelled orders for everyone to kneel. One of them reeked of alcohol as he pressed a rifle barrel against her neck. She still hears the shouts in her head-the precise tone, the cadence-so vividly that she sometimes has to stop whatever she is doing, overwhelmed by a wave of terror that feels as fresh as the moment it happened. Those memories are exceptionally clear and detailed, playing back like a film she cannot pause.

Now, in the prison, the smell of alcohol on an inmate's breath instantly makes her heart pound and her palms sweat, as if she is back at that checkpoint. Being given orders by a superior officer, especially one in uniform, sets off the same false-alarm reaction: she reacts as if she is in danger even when nothing is wrong, startling at any unexpected movement nearby. Each time she smelled that alcohol or heard a command, the thought arrived with it, settled in her chest: nowhere is safe, and she would never be ready for what came next. Because she comes to believe in those moments that the world is fundamentally dangerous and that people are not what they seem, she turns to immediate strategies to cope. She puts on loud music or a blaring television at home to drown out the auditory echoes, and she replays the checkpoint scene in her head, dwelling on how the event could have been prevented. At work, she avoids being anywhere near supervisory staff, taking long detours in the hallways and choosing her seat in the break room based on how safe and protected she feels-always with her back to the wall and a clear view of the door.

Her conviction that others are untrustworthy feeds directly into these habits: the more she doubts people, the more she avoids uniformed colleagues, and the more she ruminates on what she could have done differently, which in turn keeps her memories vivid and emotionally overwhelming. Because she had concluded that danger could come from anyone at any moment, she now scanned every face, every shift in the corridor, every raised voice - the belief itself turned ordinary routines into a landscape of potential threats. When a memory does surface-often triggered by nothing more than a sudden movement that makes her flinch-she feels so overcome that she must stop everything, and this reaction reinforces her belief that she no longer knows herself, that the person she was before the checkpoint has vanished. Her heightened threat response, such as misinterpreting a guard's routine command as a threat, brings back the auditory recall of that shouted order, and each time she panics, it further cements her appraisal that the world is a perilous place. This hypervigilance also makes her more sensitive to triggers: she now notices authority figures everywhere, scanning for them even when they are absent, and the mere sight of a uniform can set off a cascade of fear before she has time to think.

Her maladaptive strategies, meanwhile, loop back to worsen the very problems they are meant to manage. The prevention rumination keeps the checkpoint memory sharp and intrusive; the loud music she uses to distract herself temporarily numbs the fear but also prevents her from processing the event, so the threat never diminishes; and her avoidance of authority figures makes those triggers even more potent when she cannot escape them. That she still needed to replay the scene, to fill the silence with noise, to take the long way - all of it confirmed, without her ever saying it aloud, that she could not handle ordinary life, and that the world was exactly as treacherous as she feared. At work, this has concrete consequences: she has been written up twice for failing to respond to a supervisor's direct call, and her husband has grown frustrated with her constant need to sit with her back to the wall in restaurants. She finally sought help after a commanding officer's raised voice caused her to drop to her knees in the prison cafeteria, gasping and sobbing. Now, sitting in the therapist's office, she says she feels like a stranger to herself. What frightens her most is the possibility that she will never feel safe again, but she hopes that at least she can stop the cycle before it costs her her job and her marriage.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not explicitly state that triggers (e.g., smell of alcohol, uniform) lead to negative appraisals (e.g., belief that the world is dangerous); appraisals appear alongside triggers but not as a direct causal consequence.
The vignette does not show that negative appraisals increase sensitivity to triggers or bring about triggers; hypervigilance is attributed to threat rather than appraisal.
The vignette does not describe maladaptive strategies (rumination, avoidance, loud music) reinforcing or causing negative appraisals; they worsen memory, threat, and triggers but not appraisals.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not explicitly state that triggers (e.g., smell of alcohol, uniform) lead to negative appraisals (e.g., belief that the world is dangerous); appraisals appear alongside triggers but not as a direct causal consequence.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not show that negative appraisals increase sensitivity to triggers or bring about triggers; hypervigilance is attributed to threat rather than appraisal.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not describe maladaptive strategies (rumination, avoidance, loud music) reinforcing or causing negative appraisals; they worsen memory, threat, and triggers but not appraisals.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
